hero.headline: Florida property tax overhaul could dismantle children's safety net across Treasure Coast
hero.body:
A proposed property tax overhaul moving through the Florida legislature could have sweeping consequences for children's services across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties. The measure, which lawmakers are debating in Tallahassee, has raised concerns about its potential impact on local government services that depend on property tax revenue.

The property tax proposal represents a significant shift in how local services are funded throughout Florida. Lawmakers have been tweaking the details of the plan, which was originally pushed by Governor Ron DeSantis, ahead of floor votes in both chambers. The changes could affect everything from schools to social services that form the safety net for vulnerable children in local communities.

Local government officials and service providers are watching the debate closely, as property taxes fund a substantial portion of county and municipal budgets across the Treasure Coast. These revenues support school districts, child welfare programs, youth recreation services, and other programs that directly serve families. Any reduction in property tax collections could force difficult decisions about which services to maintain or cut.

The legislature is moving forward with the proposal despite concerns raised about its impact on local services. Lawmakers are also considering placing a constitutional amendment on the ballot that would expand the homestead property tax exemption, giving voters the final say on at least part of the tax restructuring effort. The timeline for final votes and implementation remains under discussion in the state capital.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years for running illegal med spa from backyard shed
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa out of a shed behind her home on the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. Mena ran the business, called Miracle Hand and Spa, without proper medical credentials and provided cosmetic procedures including Botox injections that left at least one victim with partial facial paralysis.

The case came to light in May 2025 when a victim reported to Port St. Lucie Police that she experienced partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections during a session at Mena's backyard operation. The victim, who had been referred to the business by coworkers, paid $325 for the services. When she reported the paralysis, Mena refunded the money and asked her to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the issues. After the paralysis persisted, the victim requested Mena's medical license, and Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that had actually expired in February 2024. Mena also falsely claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, Code Enforcement, the Building Department, Business Tax Division, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives found extensive evidence including medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox. The discovery revealed a full-scale illegal medical operation running out of a residential backyard structure.

Mena was convicted on nine counts including three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges for obtaining property valued at $300 or more and under $20,000, and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The sentence serves as a warning to residents to verify medical credentials before undergoing any cosmetic procedures, and authorities encourage anyone who received services from Mena to contact Port St. Lucie Police.

cards.headline: Federal Court Blocks Florida's Lawsuit Against Pediatricians Group Over Gender-Affirming Care Advocacy
cards.body:
An Illinois federal court has granted a preliminary injunction blocking Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier from pursuing an enforcement lawsuit against the American Academy of Pediatrics. The lawsuit had accused the national nonprofit pediatricians organization of deceptive trade practices, racketeering, and antitrust violations based on its advocacy for gender-affirming care for transgender youth.

The court found that the academy plausibly demonstrated Florida filed the suit to punish and suppress its protected speech. According to the court's ruling, the Florida complaint contains significant misrepresentations of the academy's policy statements and rests on a weak theory that its medical guidance constituted commercial speech. The court concluded the lawsuit appeared to have been brought in bad faith without a reasonable expectation of success.

The case represents a significant development in ongoing conflicts between Florida state government and medical organizations over policies related to transgender healthcare. The American Academy of Pediatrics is a major professional organization that provides medical guidance to pediatricians nationwide, including thousands practicing in Florida. The organization's advocacy positions on gender-affirming care have become a flashpoint in broader political debates over transgender rights and medical treatment standards.

The preliminary injunction prevents Florida from continuing its enforcement action while the underlying case proceeds. The ruling addresses First Amendment concerns about whether state enforcement powers can be used to target advocacy organizations for their policy positions. Medical professional organizations closely watch such cases as they establish precedents for how states can regulate or challenge medical guidance and professional advocacy. The decision leaves open questions about what happens next in the litigation, but for now Florida cannot proceed with its claims against the pediatricians group.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce coral reef protection fight heads to federal decision as activists rally in Martin County
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County this week after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protect.
cards.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County this week after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. The reef, found hundreds of feet below the surface, is home to more than 2,000 marine species and exists nowhere else on Earth. Unlike shallow coral that requires sunlight, the Oculina Bank thrives in deep, dark waters.

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who has dived the reef, expressed concern about the ecosystem impact. "Very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food," Gilmore said. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish." Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, joined Gilmore at the gathering to urge public involvement in saving the reef.

The proposals followed a Trump Executive order issued in April 2025 that tasked eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, believes reopening access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. "The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Zales said. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010, with just 12 active boats in 2018.

Gilmore emphasized the slow growth of the corals and their long history. "They grow very, very slowly, and they've been there for a long time," he said. Perry added, "Corals are in trouble worldwide. We shouldn't be destroying anymore." Scientists warned that reopening the reef could irreparably damage what little remains of the unique ecosystem. A final federal ruling on the fate of the Oculina Bank is expected in the coming weeks.

cards.headline: Three arrested in multi-county hardware store theft ring that hit Stuart, Fort Pierce, Jupiter
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in Operation Hammer Time, a retail theft ring that burglarized at least 40 hardware stores across 13 counties including multiple locations on the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office has arrested three men connected to a widespread retail theft operation that targeted hardware stores across Martin, St. Lucie, and Palm Beach counties between December 2025 and April 2026. Major Ruben Romero identified the suspects as Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, all Miami-Dade County residents who allegedly stole approximately $500,000 worth of property from at least 40 stores across 13 counties. Local stores hit in the operation included locations in Stuart, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter, as well as others in Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, and West Palm Beach.

According to affidavits, the crews used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash storefront glass and completed thefts within minutes, often before police arrived or alarms were triggered. The stolen goods were transported back to Miami-Dade County to be resold. The first known theft connected to the ring occurred at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025, though investigators believe additional burglaries occurred before that date. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased.

Batista is currently in Martin County Jail after being arrested in February for vehicle theft, Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. Major Romero emphasized the community impact of these crimes, noting that the thefts and property damage contribute to higher prices for residents. The suspects face charges including racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of occupied and unoccupied structures. Investigators are still searching for one additional suspect.

cards.headline: Heiress Donates Land Adjacent to Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve to Block Development
cards.body:
An heiress has purchased and donated land bordering the Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve in a move aimed at stopping future development in the ecologically sensitive area. The property donation expands protected habitat in the preserve, which serves as a critical refuge for threatened and endangered species native to Florida's coastal scrub ecosystem.

The Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve protects one of the last remaining examples of coastal scrub habitat in Martin County. The preserve is home to the threatened Florida scrub jay and gopher tortoise, along with dozens of other species that depend on this increasingly rare habitat. Development pressure has steadily reduced scrub habitat across the Treasure Coast over the past several decades.

By acquiring the adjacent parcel and transferring it to preservation, the heiress effectively blocked plans that would have allowed residential or commercial development on the property. The donation ensures the land will remain in its natural state and provides additional buffer for the existing preserve. The expanded preserve will offer more protected space for wildlife movement and plant communities that require specific fire cycles and soil conditions found only in scrub ecosystems.

The land donation represents a growing trend of private conservation efforts along the Treasure Coast, where development pressure continues to threaten remaining natural areas. The expanded Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve will be managed alongside the existing protected lands, maintaining the ecological integrity of one of Martin County's most important natural resources.

hero.headline: Florida homestead tax exemption proposal raises questions about local government revenue
hero.teaser: Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut proposal that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, requiring voter approval in November.
hero.body:
Florida lawmakers on Tuesday passed a property tax cut proposal that would dramatically increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The bill requires approval from 60% of voters in November to take effect. The measure would also lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10% to 5%.

Local experts are divided on how the proposal could affect county and municipal budgets across the Treasure Coast. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace, based in Boynton Beach, raised the possibility of new fees tied to local services. "There could potentially be non-ad valorem taxes assigned to the sheriff's office, fire rescue, some of the other things. Additionally, there may be some increased fees because the only other way that the county or the local governments can derive revenue," Wallace said. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could end up carrying more of the financial burden to offset lost revenue.

Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi offered a different perspective, suggesting the measure could actually push home prices higher. "I expect home prices could actually increase because now home buyers have more money at their disposal, and that in the past has resulted in home prices going up," Gastesi said. Realtor Danielle Blake was skeptical of that theory, pointing to interest rates as a more significant barrier to sales than property taxes alone. All four experts acknowledged there are significant unknowns about how counties and municipalities might respond to decreasing property tax revenue. If the ballot measure passes, lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee to work out the specifics in a bill to implement the changes.

The tenth anniversary provides an opportunity to remember the incident while also recognizing the resilience of the Fort Pierce community and the continued presence of the Islamic Center as an important local institution serving residents of diverse backgrounds.

cards.headline: Five hospitalized after multi-vehicle crash sparks fire on I-95 in Martin County
cards.teaser: A multi-vehicle collision on Interstate 95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park resulted in five hospitalizations and a vehicle fire Monday night.
cards.body:
Five people were transported to hospitals Monday night following a multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 in Stuart that also sparked a vehicle fire. The collision occurred just before 10 p.m. on northbound I-95 near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene and found one of the vehicles engulfed in flames, which crews quickly extinguished.

Two victims suffered traumatic injuries and were taken to area hospitals, while three others sustained minor injuries and also required medical treatment. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while the Florida Highway Patrol investigated the crash scene. As of Tuesday morning, all lanes had reopened to traffic.

The cause of the multi-vehicle collision remains under investigation by the Florida Highway Patrol. The crash created significant traffic delays during the Monday evening hours as emergency crews worked to clear the scene and assist the injured.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman loses home and irreplaceable belongings after lightning strike sparks fire
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera is displaced and seeking help after a lightning strike destroyed her Fort Pierce home last month, leaving her with no insurance and few belongings.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce resident is calling for community help after a lightning strike last month destroyed her home and left her with almost nothing. Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside and told her he believed her house was on fire. St. Lucie County Fire District firefighters responded and extinguished the flames, which were caused by a lightning strike.

Rivera, who is disabled and was recovering from neck fusion surgery at the time of the fire, lost clothes, furniture, and irreplaceable personal belongings including photographs of her late son, who passed away three years ago. The extensive damage left her home uninhabitable, with broken windows and heavy structural damage throughout. Without insurance, Rivera is now staying with her nephew while she works to rebuild her life.

A memorial outside the damaged home remains one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced. Despite the overwhelming loss, Rivera expressed gratitude that she was not inside when the lightning struck and fire broke out. A GoFundMe campaign has been established to help Rivera recover and rebuild. The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of homeowners insurance and the devastating impact lightning strikes can have on Florida homes during storm season.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood waterway
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage of a black bear swimming through the Town Park community before running toward nearby homes, marking an unusual wildlife sighting on the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police released video footage Tuesday showing a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program is monitoring the bear and may set a trap to capture and relocate it if the animal does not leave the area on its own.

Police explained that Florida's black bears become more active during this time of year while searching for food, which can lead to occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions, making Tuesday's encounter particularly noteworthy. Wildlife officials recommend that residents maintain significant distance from any bears they encounter, never approach or feed the animals, and keep children and pets away. Residents should also secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties.

During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm, avoiding running, slowly backing away while keeping the bear visible, speaking in calm and firm tones, and ensuring the animal has a clear escape route. Florida's black bear population has grown substantially in recent years following decades of conservation efforts after the species was listed as threatened. This population recovery has led to more frequent human-wildlife interactions across the state, particularly in rural areas of north and central Florida, though bears increasingly wander into neighborhoods and private properties throughout the state.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places has reopened as a new restaurant, bringing fresh energy to the downtown district.
cards.body:
The Boston House, a historic Fort Pierce landmark on South Indian River Drive, has officially reopened as a dining destination after extensive renovations that preserved its historic character while reimagining its purpose. Built in 1909 by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served various roles throughout its more than century-long history.

Co-owner Georgette Angelos said the goal is to make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy and keeping its authenticity intact. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that reference the home's past. General manager Scott Laird said the revival reflects broader momentum in downtown Fort Pierce, noting that the city has done a great job bringing new life to the area.

Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct dining experience rooted in local history, blending historic preservation with a modern atmosphere. The reopening represents both the restoration of an important local landmark and a renewed gathering place serving the Fort Pierce community. The project contributes to ongoing efforts to revitalize the downtown district and showcase the region's rich historical assets.

hero.headline: Florida property tax overhaul could dismantle children's safety net across Treasure Coast
hero.body:
A proposed property tax overhaul moving through the Florida legislature could have sweeping consequences for children's services across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties. The measure, which lawmakers are debating in Tallahassee, has raised concerns about its potential impact on local government services that depend on property tax revenue.

Local government officials and service providers are watching the debate closely, as property taxes fund a substantial portion of county and municipal budgets across the Treasure Coast. The legislature is moving forward with the proposal despite concerns raised about its impact on local services. The timeline for final votes and implementation remains under discussion in the state capital.

Legislators are working to balance the desire for tax relief with the reality of maintaining services that residents depend on daily. cards.headline: State lawmakers approve placing homestead exemption expansion on ballot
cards.teaser: The Florida legislature has approved a constitutional amendment that would expand the homestead property tax exemption, sending the question to voters.
cards.body:
Florida legislators have voted to place a constitutional amendment on the ballot that would expand the homestead property tax exemption available to residents. The measure gives voters the opportunity to decide whether to increase the exemption, which reduces the taxable value of primary residences and lowers annual property tax bills for homeowners.

The expanded exemption would benefit homeowners across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties who qualify for homestead status. Property owners must live in their home as their primary residence to claim the exemption, which provides tax relief by exempting a portion of the home's value from taxation.

By placing the question before voters as a constitutional amendment, lawmakers are allowing residents to directly decide on the tax policy change. The ballot measure will require approval from 60 percent of voters to pass and become part of the state constitution, permanently altering how homestead properties are taxed in Florida.

hero.headline: Lake Worth Beach to host arrival of 80-mile ocean paddle raising funds for cystic fibrosis research
hero.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean this June in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of endurance paddling. Participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, with spectators invited to Lake Worth Beach for a daylong celebration marking their arrival.

The event benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, established by founder Travis Suit in honor of his daughter, Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. Suit, an avid paddler, was inspired to create the crossing after learning about the natural respiratory benefits of ocean salt air. All paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, with crew or virtual participants required to raise $500. Final contributions are due July 31.

Safety measures are paramount for the overnight ocean crossing. All participants are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held.

The four-day event schedule begins June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. Thursday includes a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before the midnight launch. The foundation provides direct support for cystic fibrosis patients and families, connecting them with resources and community. More information and donation details are available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with the audience. During an early performance, he experienced an unexpected moment when a wig change went wrong, leaving him bald for an entire scene.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. hero.headline: Federal Court Blocks Florida's Lawsuit Against Pediatricians Group Over Gender-Affirming Care Advocacy
hero.body:
An Illinois federal court has granted a preliminary injunction blocking Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier from pursuing an enforcement lawsuit against the American Academy of Pediatrics. The lawsuit had accused the national nonprofit pediatricians organization of deceptive trade practices, racketeering, and antitrust violations based on its advocacy for gender-affirming care for transgender youth.

The court found that the academy plausibly demonstrated Florida filed the suit to punish and suppress its protected speech. According to the court's ruling, the Florida complaint contains significant misrepresentations of the academy's policy statements and rests on a weak theory that its medical guidance constituted commercial speech. The court concluded the lawsuit appeared to have been brought in bad faith without a reasonable expectation of success.

The case represents a significant development in ongoing conflicts between Florida state government and medical organizations over policies related to transgender healthcare. The American Academy of Pediatrics is a major professional organization that provides medical guidance to pediatricians nationwide, including thousands practicing in Florida. The organization's advocacy positions on gender-affirming care have become a flashpoint in broader political debates over transgender rights and medical treatment standards.

The preliminary injunction prevents Florida from continuing its enforcement action while the underlying case proceeds. The ruling addresses First Amendment concerns about whether state enforcement powers can be used to target advocacy organizations for their policy positions. Medical professional organizations closely watch such cases as they establish precedents for how states can regulate or challenge medical guidance and professional advocacy. The decision leaves open questions about what happens next in the litigation, but for now Florida cannot proceed with its claims against the pediatricians group.

The dispute reflects broader debates in Florida and nationally about redistricting, representation, and intraparty dynamics. hero.headline: Multi-county theft ring hit 40 hardware stores including Stuart, Fort Pierce and Jupiter in Operation Hammer Time
hero.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a retail theft ring that targeted at least 40 hardware stores across 13 counties from December 2025 to April 2026, stealing roughly $500,000 worth of property.
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in Operation Hammer Time, a multi-county retail theft ring that hit hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19; Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39; and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31 were all involved in a series of burglaries from December 2025 to April 2026. At least 40 stores across 13 counties were burglarized, with stolen goods taken back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold.

According to a Martin County Sheriff's Office affidavit, hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce and Jupiter were targeted, as were stores in Broward County. The crews would use a sledgehammer or other blunt object to smash the glass, often completing the thefts within minutes before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage to stores.

"There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are," Romero said of the impact. "People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools." Batista is connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and is in Martin County Jail, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. The suspects face charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure and burglary of an unoccupied structure.

cards.headline: Five hospitalized after multi-vehicle crash sparks fire on I-95 in Stuart

Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to the hospital, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the crash. As of Tuesday morning, all lanes have reopened.

cards.headline: Martin County activists rally to save rare deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce as federal protections rollback looms
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for t.
cards.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth. Located just off the coast of Fort Pierce, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and is home to more than 2,000 marine species. Unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive, the Oculina Bank thrives in deep, dark waters.

Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the rare reef, explained the stakes for local marine life. "Very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food," Gilmore said. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish." Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, and Gilmore urged the public to help save the reef. Scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago.

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, following a Trump Executive order issued in April 2025 that tasked regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate the fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, said reopening shrimping access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. "The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Zales said. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers dropped from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, with just 12 active boats in 2018.

"Corals are in trouble worldwide. We shouldn't be destroying anymore," Gilmore said at the gathering. Perry echoed the concern about the reef's fragile state. "They grow very, very slowly, and they've been there for a long time," Perry said. Scientists warned that reopening the reef could irreparably damage what little remains of this unique ecosystem found nowhere else on the planet. The federal agency is preparing its final ruling on the fate of the Oculina Bank protections.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
hero.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an illegal medical spa out of a shed in her backyard. The case broke open in May 2025 when a victim reported partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections at Mena's makeshift business, Miracle Hand and Spa, located at her residence in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive.

The victim, who had been referred to the business by coworkers, paid $325 for the services. When she reported the paralysis to Mena, Mena refunded the money but asked the victim to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the issues. When the paralysis persisted, the victim requested to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered certificate of phlebotomy that had expired in February 2024. Mena also told the victim she was a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's home. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox.

Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud-swindle to obtain property worth $300 or more, one count of fraud-swindle to obtain property under $20,000, and one count of use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The investigation demonstrates the serious risks of unlicensed medical procedures and the coordination between local agencies to protect public health.

cards.headline: Lightning strike destroys Fort Pierce woman's home, leaving her displaced and without irreplaceable belongings
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera lost nearly everything when lightning struck her Fort Pierce home last month, including photos of her late son and most of her possessions.
cards.body:
Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church last month to find a utility worker warning her that her house was on fire. A lightning strike had ignited flames that tore through her Fort Pierce home, and St. Lucie County District Firefighters rushed to extinguish the blaze. The damage left Rivera with broken windows, heavy interior destruction, and almost nothing salvageable.

Rivera lost clothes, furniture, and irreplaceable personal belongings, including photos of her son who passed away three years ago. She is now displaced and staying at her nephew's home while she tries to rebuild. Rivera is uninsured and was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week the fire destroyed her home. A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced.

Rivera, who is disabled, described the experience as overwhelming but expressed gratitude that she was not inside when the lightning struck. A GoFundMe has been set up to help her rebuild and recover from the loss.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination after major renovation
cards.teaser: The 1909 landmark along South Indian River Drive has been transformed into a new restaurant while preserving its historic character and ties to early Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
The Boston House, built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, has officially reopened as a dining experience after extensive renovations. Co-owner Georgette Angelos said the goal is to make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy and preserving its authenticity.

The home was originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that reflect the home's past. General manager Scott Laird said the revival reflects broader momentum in downtown Fort Pierce and the city's efforts to bring new life to the area.

Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere. The reopening marks a new chapter for both the landmark and downtown Fort Pierce as the city works to redefine its future.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood, wildlife officials monitoring
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video of a black bear swimming in the Town Park community before running toward homes, marking an unusual sighting along the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear and may set a trap to capture and relocate it if the animal does not move from the area on its own.

Police said Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, which can lead to occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions. Wildlife officials recommend maintaining significant distance from bears, never approaching them, and avoiding any attempts to feed them. Residents should keep children and pets away and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed.

Florida's black bears, once listed as threatened, have increasingly wandered into neighborhoods in recent years as the population has grown substantially following decades of conservation efforts. During unexpected encounters, officials stress remaining calm, avoiding running, slowly backing away while keeping the bear visible, and ensuring the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.headline: Make-A-Wish Foundation honors 12 local children as junior deputies at St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office
cards.teaser: Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro in a ceremony honoring young heroes facing serious medical challenges.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office honored 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation on Wednesday, swearing them in as junior deputies in a ceremony led by Sheriff Richard Del Toro. The sheriff called it one of the greatest days in his career and said the young heroes left an imprint on the department.

Among those honored were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder requiring a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save her life, enduring pain and spending time in a wheelchair. Mia said her brother made her feel safe during the frightening experience. Also sworn in was Tobias Deleon, who was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity said Tobias even stopped breathing at one point but miraculously recovered.

The junior deputies received badges, toured the sheriff's office, and saw demonstrations from the helicopter unit, SWAT team, and K-9 officers. Parents thanked law enforcement for making their children feel special and reminding them they are important members of the community.
